title: How Grocery Coupon Stacking Actually Works (Explained Simply)
creator: Tasha Robinson
description:
Store coupons, manufacturer coupons, app offers and cashback: what stacks, what doesn't, and why your coupon got rejected at the till.

This is an explainer, not a deals post. Coupon rules change by store and by state, so always check your store's coupon policy.

0:00 The four kinds of discount
1:20 How stacking works
2:40 Walking through a receipt
4:00 Common mistakes

sentences.t: Hey y'all, so I get this question constantly.
How do people walk out of the store with a cart full of food and pay like six dollars?
Today I'm going to explain how coupon stacking actually works, no hype, just the rules.
So first, there are basically four kinds of discounts, and the whole trick is knowing which ones can be combined.
Number one is a store coupon, which comes from the store itself.
Number two is a manufacturer coupon, which comes from the company that makes the product, like the cereal brand.
Number three is a digital offer in the store's app.
And number four is a cashback app, which pays you after you've already bought something.
Now, stacking.
The general rule is you can use one store coupon and one manufacturer coupon on the same item.
But you usually can't use two manufacturer coupons on one item, even if you have two of them.
Cashback apps sit outside all of that, because the store never even sees them.
Let me walk you through an actual receipt from last week so this makes sense.
At Kroger, I bought a box of cereal that was four ninety-nine on the shelf.
There was a Kroger digital coupon in the app, one dollar off when you buy two, so I bought two.
Then I had a manufacturer coupon from the Sunday paper, seventy-five cents off one box, and I used two of those, one per box.
And the store had a weekly sale where that cereal was marked down to three forty-nine anyway.
So instead of almost ten dollars, I paid about four fifty for both boxes, before cashback.
Then I scanned the receipt in Ibotta, and got another fifty cents back on each box a few days later.
So that's all four types on one product, and that's really all stacking is.
It's not magic, it's just reading the fine print on four different things at once.
Okay, now the mistakes that get people's coupons rejected.
The big one is not reading the size.
If the coupon says sixteen ounce or larger, and you grab the twelve ounce, it'll beep at the register and the cashier can't override it.
Mistake number two, expiry dates.
Paper coupons expire, and a lot of people find a coupon in a drawer from three months ago and get annoyed at the till.
Mistake three is assuming every store doubles coupons.
Some stores used to double manufacturer coupons up to a certain value, but most don't anymore, so check before you build your whole list around it.
And honestly, the biggest mistake of all is buying stuff you don't need because there's a coupon.
A dollar off something you'd never buy is not saving a dollar, it's spending three.
I only coupon for things already on my list, and that alone keeps my grocery bill sane.
So that's coupon stacking in about five minutes.
In my next video I'm going to show you how I plan a week of meals around whatever is on sale, which is where the real savings are.
Let me know what your store's coupon rules are like in the comments, because they're all a little different.
Bye for now.
